patches.entity_key: Adjectives change meaning based on position
value: Only a small set of adjectives behaves this way (ancien, cher, pauvre, propre, sale, grand, dernier)
Most adjectives keep the same meaning in either position

evidence.notes: Derived from the rule's stated condition and restriction; the list is taken verbatim from the rule.

value: A few adjectives in -e still have a distinct feminine in -esse (e.g. traître, traîtresse)

evidence.notes: The main rule has essentially no exceptions; traître/traîtresse is offered as the clearest one, with medium confidence.

value: The pronoun follows the verb only in the affirmative; in the negative it precedes the verb
Only toi, nous, and vous are used after the verb; me and te become moi and toi

evidence.notes: Both entries follow from the rule's formation and the parallel negative imperative rule.

value: par is used with most other passive verbs
de is limited to verbs of emotion or opinion whose agent is less active

evidence.notes: Derived from the rule's condition and restriction, contrasted with the par rule.

value: de replaces par after verbs of emotion or opinion
Some fixed passive expressions use de (e.g. aimé de tous)

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated counterpart rule; the fixed expression is standard usage with medium confidence.

patches.entity_key: Agreement of pronominal verbs in plus-que-parfait
value: No agreement when the reflexive pronoun is an indirect object (e.g. se parler)
Agreement is with a preceding direct object rather than the subject when such an object exists

evidence.notes: First entry follows the general pronominal agreement rule; the preceding-object override is standard usage.

value: No agreement when the direct object follows the verb
No agreement with indirect object pronouns (lui, leur)
The participle is invariable when the object is the pronoun en

evidence.notes: First entry is the stated trap; the indirect-object and en limits are standard usage.

value: Expressions like aller bien à quelqu'un take an indirect object instead of expressing movement
Comment allez-vous uses the vous form even for one person in formal address

evidence.notes: First entry comes from the listed expression aller bien à [quelqu'un]; the second is standard usage.

value: The subjunctive is not used after au cas où

evidence.notes: This is the exception stated in the rule's trap; a single entry is sufficient since the conditional is the rule itself.

value: The reflexive pronoun must match the subject
se faire and se laisser take a following infinitive, not a past participle

evidence.notes: First entry follows from the formation; the infinitive pattern comes from the listed expressions.
